title: Fiji Shows Character To Defeat Japan 34–28 In Thrilling Test Match
article_text:
The Fiji Water Flying Fijians produced a courageous and disciplined performance to defeat Japan 34–28 in a thrilling international Test match, overcoming the challenge of playing 20 minutes with 14 men to secure a memorable victory on Japanese soil.

In a contest that was evenly poised at 21–21 at halftime, Fiji demonstrated resilience, tactical discipline and composure under pressure to outlast the Brave Blossoms and deliver a winning start for newly appointed head coach Jake White.

The victory carried added significance as Japan celebrated 100 years of rugby, with Fiji spoiling the hosts’ centenary celebrations while gaining valuable momentum ahead of a demanding international campaign.

The match took a significant turn in the 34th minute when Fiji’s Motikai Murray was shown a yellow card for a dangerous tackle. The decision was subsequently upgraded to a red card.

Despite the numerical disadvantage, Fiji refused to surrender its attacking ambition or defensive intensity. With the scores locked at 21–21 at the interval, the visitors faced a difficult second half against a Japanese side determined to capitalize on its extra player.

However, Fiji displayed remarkable determination, maintaining its defensive organization while making the most of its attacking opportunities.

Tries from Kitione Salawa, captain Tevita Ikanivere, Tuidraki Samusamuvodre and Terio Tamani contributed to Fiji’s winning performance, with Isaiah Armstrong-Ravula providing conversions and Ben Volavola contributing penalty goals.

The Flying Fijians ultimately held their nerve to secure a six-point victory, underlining their ability to manage a high-pressure Test match despite significant adversity.

While Japan enjoyed a slight advantage in possession and territory, Fiji’s defensive workload and ability to force turnovers proved crucial.

According to the official full-time match statistics, Japan recorded 51 percent possession and 55 percent territory, compared with Fiji’s 49 percent and 45 percent respectively.

Fiji was required to make 146 tackles, compared with Japan’s 129, reflecting the considerable defensive pressure absorbed by the visitors.

More importantly, Fiji won 10 turnovers compared with Japan’s four, demonstrating the effectiveness of its defensive contest at the breakdown and its ability to disrupt Japanese possession.

The Flying Fijians also conceded just three penalties throughout the contest, compared with Japan’s 10; a particularly significant statistic given that Fiji played much of the match with one fewer player.

Although Japan gained more metres, recording 447 compared with Fiji’s 313, and narrowly edged the defenders-beaten count 26–23, the visitors were more effective in converting critical moments into points.

Fiji’s scrum remained solid, winning all five of its scrums, while Japan won five and lost one. The lineout presented greater challenges for the visitors, who won seven but lost six, compared with Japan’s seven won and one lost.

Ultimately, Fiji’s ability to secure turnovers, maintain discipline and manage possession during the closing stages proved decisive.

One of the most significant developments in the Flying Fijians’ victory was the dramatic improvement in their discipline compared with the two sides’ previous encounter in the Pacific Nations Cup last month.

During the PNC finals, which Japan won 20–15, Fiji conceded 16 penalties and received a yellow card, with repeated infringements placing the team under considerable pressure.

However, in their latest encounter, Fiji reduced its penalty count to just three, an impressive 81.25 percent reduction, representing 13 fewer penalties than in the previous meeting.

The improvement was particularly noteworthy given that Fiji was reduced to 14 players following Murray’s 34th-minute yellow card, which was subsequently upgraded to red.

Despite the numerical disadvantage, the Flying Fijians maintained their defensive structure and avoided repeated infringements, limiting Japan’s opportunities to gain territory or score points from penalties.

Fiji also improved its turnover count from nine in the PNC encounter to 10 in the latest Test, reinforcing the effectiveness of its defensive pressure and breakdown contest.

The contrast between the two performances was significant. Just one month after suffering a five-point defeat, Fiji returned to defeat the same opposition by six points, scoring 34 points compared with 15 in their previous meeting.

The result represented an 11-point turnaround in the winning margin between the two encounters.

For head coach Jake White, the improvement in discipline provides an encouraging early indication of the team’s ability to execute a more controlled and structured approach to international rugby.

While one performance cannot establish a lasting trend, the reduction in penalties, combined with Fiji’s improved game management in the closing stages, suggests that the players are responding positively to the coaching staff’s emphasis on control and decision-making.

The challenge for the Flying Fijians will now be to maintain these standards against France, Ireland and Italy, where discipline and the ability to manage pressure will be equally important.

For head coach Jake White, the victory represented more than just a successful result. It was an encouraging first step towards developing a more controlled and tactically disciplined Flying Fijians side.

Returning to international coaching after a 20-year absence, White expressed both excitement and relief following the final whistle.

“I’m very excited. I mean, I’m relieved as well. We just had a short time with this team,” White said.

“I haven’t coached international rugby for 20 years, so I was very excited. I was like a little boy in a candy store today.”

White acknowledged the importance of beginning the tour with a victory, particularly given the limited preparation time available to the coaching staff.

“I’m glad the boys stuck it out because, obviously, it’s an important win for us to start our tour with a win.”

title: Springbok Women back set-piece strength and squad depth for historic Ireland clash
article_text:
The Springbok Women face Ireland for the first time in 20 years at Athlone Stadium tomorrow (15:00), and for Vainah Ubisi the focus is simple: match Ireland’s set-piece power and take the fight to them at source.

Ireland, ranked fifth in the world, arrive with a reputation for powerful lineouts and a strong kicking game, and Ubisi says the Boks have spent the week planning to disrupt exactly that.

“As much as they are a good set-piece team, we also are. I think we have the same strength,” she said.

“Our plan going into tomorrow’s game is to kill them at source, close them middle and back on the lineouts, and make sure they don’t get clean ball.

“On the scrums as well, we want to scrum for penalties and take their scrums. Whatever they bring tomorrow, we are ready for it.”

South Africa, ranked 10th, are the lower-ranked side on paper, but Ubisi was quick to point to the squad’s own standards.

“The preparations have been focusing on what we want to achieve this weekend, because we obviously built into us being the number one in the world.”

Captain Sizophila Solontsi framed the occasion differently, not as a historic milestone, but as a new beginning.

“Most of the people that played 20 years ago are no longer here, and we acknowledge that. They paved the way for us,” she said.

“But going into this match, it’s more of a fresh start: the new generation and all the growth that has happened. A new chapter.”

She welcomed the challenge of facing a top-five side the current squad has never met.

“It’s always more exciting to play a higher-ranked team than us, because we get to challenge ourselves and see where we are as a group. The coaches will also know how we step up to that level.”

Solontsi will take the captaincy with Babalwa Latsha ruled out through injury and the front row reshuffled, a situation she says the squad’s development pathways have prepared them for.

“With the academy sides, under-20s and now the SA Schools, anyone who comes into the system can slot in easily,” she said.

“The new front row is not necessarily new players; it’s players who have played in the team before and are familiar with the system. We’ve seen at training this week, they just jumped in.”

She added that the leadership group is backing each other through the change.

“Whoever is not available, the next person is available to step up.”

There is also a milestone to celebrate, with Yonela Ngxingolo set to earn her 50th cap off the bench, becoming only the second woman in South Africa to reach the mark after the retired Nolusindiso Booi.

“It’s a very big thing for our group, that we can actually have people that reach 50,” Solontsi said.

“It shows her resilience within the system and just fighting to stay within the system and keep playing. It’s a very big achievement for us and the team as a whole.”

For a squad building toward 2029, tomorrow is both a measuring stick and a fresh start.

title: Wallaroos complete Scotland sweep as retiring Smith gets standing ovation despite red
article_text:
The Wallaroos completed their three-game sweep over Scotland with a 38-31 win on Friday in a spicy contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Canberrabut again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it. The hosts received four yellow cards, with the retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sent to the sin bin and it could have been far uglier if the Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs’ accusations of biting had been verified on review. But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich’s forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

The Australian prop Eva Karpani was shown a yellow card for a high shot in her milestone game on her 50th cap, while the impressive teenage fly-half Waiaria Ellis was also sent to the sin bin for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for the retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation despite being sent off. “I’m really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess,” Smith said as she embraced her daughter, Ruby, after the match. “She’s been there since day one,” said Smith of her daughter. “Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and put the hard work in.”

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after making her debut in 2018. “It’s created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for,” she said. “I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can’t be what you can’t see.”

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against Scotland. The Wallaroos are now out of action until the side transitions to a full-time operation next year under their new coach, Sione Fukofuka, who has previously coached Scotland.

Australia led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries. The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when the captain, Siokapesi Palu, finished a long-range effort. But after losing Karpani and then Smith, Scotland surged back into the match, although they were unable to find the match-tying converted try on the final play.

title: Guzmán Barreiro Names strong Uruguay Roster to face Spain, Zimbabwe and Portugal
article_text:
The recently appointment Guzmán Barreiro has named a strong Uruguayan roster for upcoming international duty. Los Teros will face Spain, Zimbabwe and Portugal in Europe in November as part of the 2026 World Rugby Nations Cup.

The three match tour will be Barreiro’s second assignment after he became head coach. He took over ahead of the 2026 Americas Rugby Championship (ARC). His tour to Europe is the tour to tick boxes less than a year out from Rugby World Cup 2027. Uruguay will face Ireland, Portugal, and Scotland in Australia 2027.

When compared to the Uruguayan roster from July, the November selection is stronger. It has been bolstered by the inclusion of hooker Germán Kessler, and tight head prop Ignacio Péculo who missed out on July selection due to injuries. Fellow front-rowers Guillermo Pujadas and Francisco Suárez remain sidelined with long term injuries.

The other notable returnee is Manuel Leindekar. The second-rower took over from Andrés Vilaseca as captain only to be rested for July this year as part of an arrangement with his new club in France, Grenoble.

The roster does not come without players missing from selection. In addition to the aforementioned Francisco Suárez, Santiago Cagnone is a second loose head prop not selected. He plays his rugby for Benfica a Agronomía in Portugal but is uncapped.

At hooker, Joaquín Myszka misses out after suspension following the gruesome late tackle that caused a year out of rugby for Chile’s Emilio Shea. There is no place for Máximo Lamelas who debuted for Uruguay against Hong Kong in July.

Only two tight head props made the cut. This sees a low total of just seven front-rowers. Diego Arbelo remains out of favor. Meanwhile, Lucas Porcelli, who debuted for Uruguay in July has not been selected by Barreiro.

Back-rowers Santiago Civetta and Carlos Deus are notably missing from the roster. Both were regulars over a sustained period and had busy campaigns for Uruguay at Rugby World Cup 2023. Rookie Arturo Ten Hoever misses out after debuting against Georgia in July.

The world-class Santiago Arata is missing. Uruguay’s most famous player is not involved but will be free for Uruguay for busy involvement before and during Rugby World Cup 2027. Fellow scrum-half, Santiago Álvarez has also not been included. He has been the regular starter in place of Arata this RWC cycle.

Veteran fly half Felipe Etcheverry is not on the roster nor is Juan Zuccarino or Francisco Landauer. Etcheverry was the starting fly half for a number of years while Zuccarino had been his understudy for Peñarol before injury. Landauer made his debut last November against Romania.

Center Franco Scaldaferri debuted for Uruguay against Hong Kong in July but misses out on November selection. He was one of many new players selected under Rodolfo Ambrosio. Fullback Francisco González Capdevila is another example. He misses out and there is no place for Bautista Basso, and Baltazar Amaya who were starting outside backs last World Cup.

title: Alcaraz faces Khachanov test in Vienna opener; Zverev meets Landaluce
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz will likely have little time to find his indoor hard-court feet at the Erste Bank Open.

The No. 3 player in the PIF ATP Rankings has been drawn against former Top-10 star and recent US Open semi-finalist Karen Khachanov at the ATP 500 event in Vienna. Alcaraz, who will compete in the Austrian capital for the first time since 2021, will be seeking a fast start to his European indoor swing after his third-round exit to Zizou Bergs at the Rolex Shanghai Masters.

Although Alcaraz will be wary of the threat posed by seven-time ATP Tour champion Khachanov, the Spaniard will enter the Vienna encounter with a 6-0 lead in the pair’s Lexus ATP Head2Head series. Should he extend his perfect record against Khachanov, Alcaraz would face Nikoloz Basilashvili or home wild card Jurij Rodionov in the second round, while seventh seed Tommy Paul is a potential quarter-final opponent.

Daniil Medvedev, who will compete in the Almaty semi-finals on Saturday, is also in Alcaraz’s half of the draw. The former World No. 1 is currently sixth in the PIF ATP Live Race To Turin, and will know that a deep run in Vienna can bolster his Nitto ATP Finals qualification hopes.

Alexander Zverev is the top seed in Vienna, where the German could also complete his journey to becoming World No. 1 for the first time. If he reaches the quarter-finals in Austria, Zverev will be guaranteed to rise to top spot on 2 November: He begins his title tilt at the Wiener Stadthalle against #NextGenATP wild card Martin Landaluce, while Brandon Nakashima and Tallon Griekspoor are his potential second-round opponents.

A trio of Nitto ATP Finals hopefuls — Flavio Cobolli, Alex de Minaur and Frances Tiafoe — feature in Zverev’s half of the draw. Sixth seed Tiafoe is a potential quarter-final opponent for the German, but faces a blockbuster opening match against Lorenzo Musetti. Fourth seed Cobolli, who starts against Grigor Dimitrov, and fifth seed De Minaur, who begins by facing a qualifier, are seeded to meet in the last eight.

title: Pang Ron-Pei Jing reach second World Tour final
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Independent mixed doubles pair Hoo Pang Ron-Lai Pei Jing booked their second World Tour final of the season after clearing their French Open semi-final on Saturday.

The world No. 31 overcame China's world No. 6 Guo Xin Wa–Chen Fang Hui 21-13, 21-9 at Arena Grand Paris.

Pang Ron-Pei Jing had reached their maiden World Tour final together at the China Masters last month, finishing runners-up to China's Feng Yan Zhe-Huang Dong Ping, before making the Denmark Open semi-finals last week.

They will face either Yan Zhe-Dong Ping or France's Thom Gicquel-Delphine Delrue in Sunday's final.

title: French Open: Akechi on Dream Run
article_text:
Before this week, Hina Akechi had never gone beyond the second round at a Super 750.

Now the Japanese has stormed into the YONEX French Open 2026 semifinals – without dropping a game.

Michelle Li, second seed Wang Zhi Yi and fifth seed Putri Kusuma Wardani – all higher-ranked, swept aside in Paris.

“I am very happy but also tired,” giggled Akechi after her 21-17 21-18 win over Wardani on Friday.

“I finished late, so I ate a lot and tried to stretch well. I wouldn’t say I am a good cook but I bought my rice cooker with me and I made some food with it. My confidence is pretty high after beating two top players in the tournament. I’m very excited to play in my first Super 750 semifinal. It’s my first time playing Pusarla V.Sindhu too. She’s tall so I think she may have me run a lot in the match.”

France’s hopes remain firmly intact after Alex Lanier came through an all-French quarter-final against Toma Junior Popov to reach the last four on home soil.

The reigning world champion recovered from a game down to defeat Popov 16-21 21-16 21-16, raising his level when it mattered most to keep his title bid alive in Paris.

Lanier admitted he found himself battling more than just his opponent.

“I told my coach that I was definitely stressed. Mentally I didn’t feel comfortable on court and, especially physically, my legs were not responding the way I wanted. I was doubting myself a lot. After losing the first game, a few thoughts crossed my mind. Should I give up? Should I just go home, go to the beach or get some rest?

“But I’m not like that anymore. I’m trying to push through those moments. It’s a good experience for me to learn how to go that far.”

Having come through his toughest test of the week, the 21-year-old will now face Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah, who booked his place in a maiden Super 750 semifinal with a 21-15 21-13 victory over Chi Yu Jen. The world No.28 acknowledged the significance of the achievement.

“I am very happy. Reaching a Super 750 semifinal for the first time is another milestone for me this year. I didn’t expect it, but I always learn from every match I play, evaluating both my wins and losses. I try to take the positives from every opportunity and I’m grateful to have made it this far.”

Ubaidillah revealed he grew up idolising some of the sport’s greatest names.

“Taufik Hidayat, Lin Dan and Lee Chong Wei are my role models. Their journeys have inspired me since I was young. Right now, though, I see Alex Lanier as a player who is building an excellent career.”

The semifinal will mark the pair’s first meeting.

Christo Popov continued France’s impressive day in Paris, beating Kodai Naraoka 21-15 21-16 to reach the semifinals.

Reigning world champions Thom Gicquel and Delphine Delrue soon followed, fighting past Wu Guan Xun/Lee Chia Hsin 21-23 21-12 21-14 to keep home hopes burning on another memorable day for the hosts.

title: Hye-Jin Choi's Front-Nine 28 Fuels Charge Into Contention at BMW Ladies Championship
article_text:
Megan McCrea is the Manager of Digital Operations. Megan is in her second year with the LPGA, working with the LPGA and Epson Tours to manage, develop, maintain, and update website content.

Hye-Jin Choi of the Republic of Korea played the front nine at Pine Beach Golf Links in 8-under 28 and finished with a 6-under 66 on Saturday to move into a tie for second at the BMW Ladies Championship in Haenam-gun, Jeollanam-do.

Choi, 27, is 13-under 203 through three rounds, four shots behind leader Haeran Ryu, who stands at 17-under 199 with one round remaining.

Starting the third round T11 at 7-under 137, Choi made six birdies and an eagle on the par-5 sixth over her first nine holes. The run carried her to 15-under at the turn and put pressure on Ryu at the top of the leaderboard.

“I had a really good score on the front nine,” Choi said. “I felt good about my ball-striking early on, so I was able to play confidently and make a lot of birdie putts.”

She added a birdie at the par-4 10th to reach 16-under, but the back nine was bumpier. Choi finished the round with eight birdies, one eagle, two bogeys and a double bogey at the par-5 17th, which cost her momentum down the stretch.

“I missed my second shot on the par-5 17th,” said Choi. “Looking back, I think I misjudged the shot.”

Her ball-striking was the story of the day. Choi hit 17 of 18 greens in regulation and 11 of 14 fairways, averaging 234.0 yards off the tee, and needed 29 putts. Her approach play has been a strength all season: she ranks 14th on the LPGA Tour in strokes gained approach at +0.79 per round and eighth in strokes gained total at +1.51.

Choi has made 18 cuts in 23 starts this season with five top-10 finishes: T8 at Honda LPGA Thailand, T5 at the Blue Bay LPGA, T3 at the Mizuho Americas Open, second at the Dow Championship and solo second last week at the Buick LPGA Shanghai. She is still seeking her first LPGA Tour victory.

With 18 holes left, Choi plans to keep her approach simple.

“Rather than thinking too much about competing for the title, I just want to focus as much as possible on each shot,” she said.

title: Chandler Blanchet, Kensei Hirata share 36-hole lead at Butterfield Bermuda Championship heading into windy weekend
article_text:
SOUTHAMPTON, Bermuda (AP) – Chandler Blanchet turned trouble off the tee into a birdie on the 18th hole, giving him a 4-under 67 on Friday and a share of the lead with Kensei Hirata of Japan going into what figures to be a windy weekend at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship.

Hirata played bogey-free at Port Royal Golf Course for a 64 to join Blanchet at 13-under 129. Hirata had never shared the lead after any round in his rookie season on the PGA Tour.

Blanchet tugged his drive on the par-4 closing hole and was hoping it would land in the bunker to at least give him a reasonable lie. It cleared the sand, but his golf ball was on a slight slope above his feet, leaving him a blind shot to a front pin.

The wedge came out perfectly, settling 5 feet away for a final birdie.

“Had a pretty uphill, above-the-feet lie and completely blind shot,” Blanchet said. “It was kind of a fun creative one, which I think you’ve got to be pretty solid at this week with the wind. Can't just take your stock shots. So it was a good way to end it.”

Chandler Blanchet drains 6-foot birdie putt on No. 18 at Butterfield Bermuda

Seamus Power, who won Butterfield Bermuda in 2022 when the Irishman was among the top 50 in the world, shook off a poor finish to the opening round with a bogey-free 64. He was one shot behind, along with Corey Conners (67), Eric Cole (65), Ben Silverman (67) and Danny Walker, who birdied his last two holes for a 67.

Wind is the strongest defense of Port Royal, and it has not been up to full strength through two rounds. That much was evident by the scoring, so low that the 36-hole cut came at 5-under 137.

Among those missing the cut were defending champion Adam Schenk and Chandler Phillips, who came into the tournament at No. 98 in the FedExCup Fall standings. This is the fourth event of the fall, leaving four more tournaments for players to finish in the top 100 and keep full status for 2027.

Power is at No. 103, so a big weekend would go a long way. He finished at No. 114 a year ago and still managed to get into most tournaments (except the Signature Events).

Seamus Power sinks 10-foot birdie putt on No. 18 at Butterfield Bermuda

“But it was the unknowns,” he said. "Not knowing where I was going to get in and when I was going to get in was the tough part. Trying to get back into that top 100, get yourself back to full status, I just feel like you’re in a better more comfortable spot starting off in January.

“So like that’s going to be the big goal.”

The immediate goal is to handle the wind, which was forecast to be gusting stronger than it has all week at Port Royal.

“The weather’s going to be pretty difficult, so try and stay patient and excuse a few bad shots here and there, some wind gusts,” Cole said. “Just try and stay patient and have fun with it a little bit.”

title: Holder Rybakina sets up Fernandez clash in Ningbo final
World No. 1 Seo Seung-jae-Kim Won-ho Extend Title Drought to Nine Tournaments
article_text:
[OSEN=Jeong Seung-woo Reporter] The world ranking remains No. 1. However, it has been a long time since news of a championship victory was heard. The South Korean men’s doubles badminton flagbearers Seo Seung-jae-Kim Won-ho (both Samsung Life Insurance) have once again failed to win a title. This time, they did not even reach the semifinals.

Seo Seung-jae-Kim Won-ho pair lost in the quarterfinals of the 2026 Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Tour France Open (Super 750) men’s doubles held at Arena Bercy in Paris, France, on the 24th (Korean time) to Malaysia’s Goh Jae Wei-Nur Izzudin pair (world No. 5) with a game score of 0-2 (15-21, 18-21).

The match lasted only 36 minutes. It was a defeat that made their status as world No. 1 seem meaningless. They struggled against the opponents’ fast and accurate net play. After losing the first game 15-21, the Seo-Kim pair attempted a comeback in the second game but failed to reverse the momentum. When trailing 18-20, they faced additional misfortune as their opponent’s smash hit the net and fell back into their court.

Ultimately, they lost the second game 18-21 and ended the tournament there. A week earlier, they had also failed to advance beyond the semifinals at the Denmark Open. At the France Open, they packed their bags one round earlier. More concerning was that this result was not a temporary slump.

This marks their ninth consecutive tournament without a title.

The Seo-Kim pair reigned as the absolute powerhouse in world men’s doubles just last year. After reuniting in early 2025, the duo won their first tournament, the Malaysia Open, and went on to dominate major events such as the All England Open, Indonesia Open, World Championships, France Open, and BWF World Tour Finals.

They won an astonishing 11 tournaments last year and claimed the world No. 1 ranking. Their momentum continued into early this year, with victories at the Malaysia Open, All England Open, and Asian Championships, reaffirming their status as the world’s strongest pair.

The situation changed in May. They lost 0-2 to India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy-Chirag Shetty pair in the semifinals of the Singapore Open. Then, in the semifinals of the Indonesia Open, they were defeated by the same Goh Jae Wei-Nur Izzudin pair who eliminated them at the France Open.

Since then, they have not won a title. At the July Japan Open and China Open, they reached the finals twice but lost both times to Indonesia’s Fajar Alfian-Muhammad Riki pair. They climbed to the final stage but failed to overcome the final hurdle.

At the August World Championships, they lost in the semifinals to Malaysia’s Soo Teck Zhi-Aaron Chia pair and had to settle for a bronze medal.

Their slump became more pronounced in September. At the China Masters, they were defeated 0-2 in the first round by Indonesia’s Leo Carnoto-Daniel Martin pair, who were ranked 59th at the time. It was a shocking result for the world No. 1 pair to exit in the opening match.

The situation did not improve at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. They faced the Carnoto-Martin pair again in the semifinals and lost 0-2 once more. They had been defeated by the same opponents twice in a row.

On the 17th, they lost 0-2 to the Soo Teck Zhi-Aaron Chia pair in the semifinals of the Denmark Open. Then, at the France Open, they failed to overcome the Malaysian pair, extending their title drought to nine consecutive tournaments.

The issue is not merely their inability to win. Over the past nine tournaments, the Seo-Kim pair recorded two runner-up finishes and five third-place results. Their performance has not completely collapsed; they have consistently remained competitive enough to reach the upper ranks.

The problem lies in their repeated losses to the same types of opponents at critical moments when competing for the title. Their weaknesses are particularly evident against Southeast Asian players. They have repeatedly failed to cross the championship threshold after losing to Indonesian and Malaysian pairs.

It is hard to ignore criticism that they are struggling to adapt to fast net play, unconventional attacks, and sudden changes in speed. Interestingly, during the same period, they maintained a perfect record against Chinese and Japanese players. They still possess the competitiveness befitting world No. 1, but they have yet to find a solution when facing specific opponents.

The same was true in the quarterfinals of the France Open. The Goh Jae Wei-Nur Izzudin pair had previously defeated the Seo-Kim pair at the Indonesia Open in June. Although they met again after about four months, the result did not change. In fact, they lost both games in just 36 minutes, suffering a complete defeat.

Given their world No. 1 ranking, the disappointment is inevitable.

Of course, being world No. 1 does not guarantee victory in every tournament. In men’s doubles, the gap between top players is narrow, and results can vary depending on opponents’ tactics and daily performance.

The pair that swept 11 tournaments last year has now gone nine tournaments without a title. The title drought has lasted long enough that it cannot be dismissed as a mere temporary slump.

Moreover, the opponents who have defeated them keep reappearing. This demonstrates that maintaining the world No. 1 ranking and defeating key rivals to claim championships are separate challenges.

The Seo-Kim pair are considered South Korea’s main medal contenders for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. However, if their current trend continues, it will be difficult to be optimistic about their gold medal prospects.

title: 2026 Pan Pacific Open Draw: Alex Eala gets favourable start as Elena Rybakina, Maja Chwalinska learn paths
article_text:
Elena Rybakina, Maja Chwalinska and Alex Eala are all set to star at the 2026 Pan Pacific Open, and the draw for the WTA 500 event is now out.

Main draw action on the outdoor hard courts of the Ariake Coliseum in Tokyo will get underway on Monday 26 October and conclude on Sunday 1 November.

This year’s Pan Pacific Open will be the 52nd edition of the prestigious tournament in Tokyo, and it is the final WTA 500 tournament on the 2026 calendar.

Belinda Bencic is the reigning champion, having beaten Linda Noskova in the 2025 final, and the Swiss star is set to defend her crown.

Six players have withdrawn from Tokyo: Jessica Pegula, Elina Svitolina, Iga Swiatek, Marta Kostyuk, Iva Jovic and Anna Kalinskaya.

The Tokyo draw features 28 players, including eight seeds: Elena Rybakina, Maja Chwalinska, Diana Shnaider, Belinda Bencic, Elise Mertens, Sorana Cirstea, Naomi Osaka and Alex Eala. The top four seeds receive a first round bye.

World No 1 Rybakina is the only top 10 player in the draw, and she will begin her campaign with a second round match against either Maria Sakkari or a qualifier.

The three-time Grand Slam champion is then projected to face fifth seed Mertens in the quarter-finals and No 4 seed Bencic in the semi-finals.

Defending champion Bencic will play either Ann Li or Ekaterina Alexandrova in her opening match, while she could meet sixth seed Cirstea in the last eight.

In the bottom half, No 2 seed Chwalinska will face either Wang Xinyu or a qualifier in her first match.

The Polish star, who won the Wuhan Open last week, could face seventh seed Naomi Osaka or the unseeded Jasmine Paolini in the quarter-finals.

Osaka and Paolini will meet in a blockbuster first round match, with the winner to play wildcard Mia Pohankova or a qualifier in the second round.

The player who progresses from the quarter featuring Chwalinska, Osaka and Paolini is projected to meet No 3 seed Shnaider or No 8 seed Eala in the semi-finals.

Shnaider will begin her campaign with a second round match against Nikola Bartunkova or a qualifier.

Eala will face world No 308 Mika Stojsavljevic — a 17-year-old British wildcard who is the lowest-ranked player in the draw — in the opening round.

The Filipina could then play Talia Gibson or a qualifier in the second round before a potential quarter-final showdown with Shnaider — who she lost to at the Ningbo Open this week.

title: WeAreNinety appoints client services director
article_text:
Manchester-based sports marketing agency WeAreNinety has appointed Alastair Henderson as client services director as it marks four years in business.

Alastair joins from Liverpool FC, where he oversaw major commercial partnerships, bringing more than 20 years’ experience across sports sponsorship, marketing and partnership management.

His career includes seven years as sports marketing director for football at adidas, alongside senior roles with the Glasgow 2014 Commonwealth Games, sponsorship agency Fast Track, E.ON UK and Wickes.

In his new role, Alastair will lead client services across WeAreNinety’s work with sports clubs, brands and athletes, covering sponsorship, activation, public relations, influencer marketing and creative production.

His appointment comes as the independent agency continues to expand its senior team and develop its offering across sports and athlete marketing.

Alastair said: “I’m really excited to be joining WeAreNinety at such an important stage in its growth.

“As a forward-thinking, full-service sports marketing agency, it has real ambition, and I’m looking forward to working with Charlie and the team to support both existing and new clients while helping to drive the next phase of the business.

“Having worked across brands, agencies, rights holders and major events, I’m looking forward to bringing that experience to the agency and helping deliver partnerships that create real value for clients.”

Charlie Weir, founder of WeAreNinety, added: “We’re absolutely thrilled to welcome Alastair to the team.

“Landing someone of his calibre is a real statement of where WeAreNinety is heading.

“Alastair has delivered partnerships for adidas, the Commonwealth Games and Liverpool FC, so he's sat in every seat our clients sit in.

“He raises the bar for how we look after the brands, clubs and talent we work with, and he's a great person to build the next chapter with.”

Krueger Tops Li, Returns to Osaka Final
article_text:
Ashlyn Krueger continues to turn Osaka into her happy space.

Krueger toppled top-seeded compatriot Ann Li 6-4, 6-7(4), 6-3, to reach her first final of the year at the Japan Open.

The 2023 Osaka champion Krueger improved to 10-2 lifetime at the tournament where she won her maiden title.

World No. 55 Krueger scored her 13th career Top 25 victory to advance to her first final since she was runner-up to Belinda Bencic at the 2025 Abu Dhabi.

Krueger broke to open the final set and backed up the break at 15. The 22-year-old Dallas native closed in two hours, 13 minutes.

The 2026 US Open doubles finalist Krueger will play Katerina Siniakova for the title.

Doubles world No. 1 Siniakova swept Briton Katie Boulter 6-1, 6-4, in today’s second semifinal.

Siniakova, who partnered Taylor Townsend to the 2026 US Open doubles championship, will play for her sixth career singles title tomorrow.
